speaker: Ilya Sutskever
title: Ilya Sutskever – We're moving from the age of scaling to the age of research
question: In frontier LLM training, why has traditional competitive self-play failed to become a general-purpose paradigm despite its promise for data-free scaling?
guest: The reason why I thought self-play was interesting is because it offered a way to create models using compute only without data. If you think data is the ultimate bottleneck, then using compute only is very interesting. Now, the thing is that self-play, at least the way it was done in the past when you have agents that somehow compete with each other, is only good for developing a certain set of skills. It is too narrow. It's only good for negotiation, conflict, certain social skills, strategizing, that kind of stuff. So if you care about those skills, then self-play will be useful. Now, actually, I think that self-play did find a home, just in a different form. Things like debate, prover-verifier, or having an LLM as a judge that is incentivized to find mistakes in your work. You could say this is not exactly self-play, but it is a related adversarial setup that people are doing.

points.core: Self-play originally appealed because compute could generate training signal without external data.
points.note: Accept: self-play promised compute-only improvement when human training data is the bottleneck. Do not credit: generic praise of AlphaGo or game-playing RL without connecting it to overcoming the data bottleneck.

points.core: Symmetric competitive self-play only develops a narrow slice of strategic conflict skills.
points.note: Accept: agents competing head-to-head mainly cultivate zero-sum or adversarial skills like strategizing, negotiation, or conflict rather than broad general capabilities. Do not credit: generic claims that language is not a game without specifying the narrowness of learned skills.

points.core: Modern LLM labs adapted self-play into asymmetric setups where verifiers hunt mistakes.
points.note: Accept: self-play evolved into prover-verifier games, debate, or adversarial LLM-as-a-judge critics incentivized to catch errors in a generator's work. Do not credit: generic mentions of RLHF or synthetic data without the adversarial error-finding structure.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Competitive self-play worked in Go, chess, and Dota because those domains are closed, two-player zero-sum games with a cheap, unambiguous win signal and a minimax solution that self-play provably approaches. Most of what we want from LLMs has none of those properties.

First, there is no ground-truth verifier for open-ended language tasks. Without a reliable referee, the reward comes from a learned judge or the opponent itself, and agents learn to exploit the judge rather than become more capable.

Second, most useful tasks are not zero-sum. Outside zero-sum settings, self-play has no convergence guarantee toward anything humans value; it can drift into degenerate equilibria, cycling strategies, collusion, or private conventions that beat the opponent but don't transfer to real tasks or human-interpretable language.

Third, adversarial curricula tend to collapse: the task-proposer generates problems that are either trivial, impossible, or narrowly adversarial, so diversity and difficulty don't scale sensibly without human-data grounding.

As a result, self-play has succeeded only in verifiable niches (formal maths, code with tests, games), while frontier training relies on human data plus RL against verifiable rewards.

points.why: The response never explains that self-play promised to turn compute into training signal without external data.
The response describes how competition can produce nontransferable strategies, but does not claim that it mainly develops a narrow set of strategic conflict skills.
The learned judge appears as a reward source that agents can exploit, with no description of a verifier incentivized to catch errors in a generator’s work.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Traditional competitive self-play succeeded in games like Go and chess because those environments are closed, zero-sum, and governed by exact, unhackable rules with unambiguous outcomes. General-purpose language tasks lack these properties: open-ended writing, analysis, and assistance are cooperative rather than strictly adversarial, and have no formal rulebook to ground truth. When frontier LLM training substitutes a learned reward model or LLM judge for an exact verifier—as in adversarial debate or generator-critic loops—competitive pressure rapidly induces reward hacking. Rather than becoming more accurate, models exploit evaluator blind spots, optimizing for superficial persuasiveness, verbosity, or subtle obfuscation. Ungrounded competition also breeds mode collapse, cyclic strategy dynamics, and linguistic drift, producing brittle behaviors misaligned with human communication. Moreover, pure self-play cannot create new world knowledge or reliably adjudicate open-ended problems beyond a model's existing competence. Consequently, self-play has proven effective mainly in externally verifiable niches—such as mathematics, executable code, and formal theorem proving—rather than becoming a universal training paradigm.

points.why: The response explains why self-play worked in games but omits its promise of generating training signals from compute alone when external data is scarce.
The response contrasts zero-sum games with cooperative language tasks but never explains that head-to-head competition mainly develops a narrow set of adversarial skills.
The response cites debate and generator–critic loops as settings for reward hacking without explaining that these adaptations use adversarial critics to find errors in a generator’s work.

noweb.answer: Traditional competitive self-play thrives in games like Go and chess because those environments are closed, zero-sum, and governed by deterministic, unhackable rules with exact win conditions. Open-ended language tasks lack an objective ground-truth verifier. When frontier LLM training replaces fixed environment rules with a learned judge or adversarial opponent—such as in debate or proposer-solver setups—optimization quickly succumbs to reward hacking. Rather than becoming more truthful or capable, competing models exploit subtle blind spots in the evaluator, converging on persuasive sophistry, non-stationary cycling, or mode collapse. Unconstrained multi-agent interaction also induces language drift, pulling generations away from natural, human-aligned communication toward brittle, idiosyncratic patterns. Moreover, while self-play can sharpen search and reasoning over closed rules, it cannot manufacture new empirical world knowledge or deduce nuanced human preferences without external grounding. Consequently, post-training compute scaling in frontier models has succeeded mainly against deterministic external verifiers in formal domains like mathematics and code, whereas open-ended competitive self-play remains too unstable and ungrounded to serve as a general-purpose paradigm.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Competitive self-play worked in Go, chess and StarCraft because those games give you a fixed, zero-sum objective and a perfect referee: the rules decide who won, so two copies of a model can keep improving against each other without human data. General language tasks have neither of these, and that is the main reason it hasn't spread to frontier LLM training.

Without a verifiable win condition, the "opponent" or judge has to be a learned model. The policy then learns to exploit the judge's blind spots (reward hacking) instead of getting more capable. Adversarial setups also tend to reward persuasion, obfuscation or degenerate tricks over correctness. Language can drift away from human-readable text, and outputs lose diversity. Proposer-solver loops in recent work such as SPIRAL, Absolute Zero, R-Zero and SPICE often plateau or become unstable after a few iterations. In those loops, the generated tasks drift toward what is easy for the model to solve or verify, not what is useful, because nothing ties them to real-world value. Strategies can also cycle without real progress, since skill in open domains isn't transitive.

So self-play mostly survives in narrow, verifiable niches like math, code and games. Elsewhere it is anchored by external checkers or human-grounded data instead of serving as a standalone, data-free scaling paradigm.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Traditional competitive self-play thrives in closed, zero-sum games like Go or StarCraft, where exact rules supply an unambiguous, incorruptible win signal. General-purpose language modeling lacks those conditions. Most real-world tasks—such as research, open-ended writing, or nuanced decision-making—are neither zero-sum nor objectively verifiable. Without an external ground-truth arbiter, competing copies of an LLM end up judging or exploiting one another's shared blind spots, leading to reward hacking, persuasive hallucinations, and language drift rather than genuine capability gains. Even when adversarial games are constructed, strictly competitive objectives often incentivize uncooperative or degenerate strategies that transfer poorly to helpful human interaction, while non-stationary opponents cause training instability and early plateaus. Finally, self-play cannot generate new empirical knowledge about the world; without external grounding, iterating on self-generated outputs amplifies errors and narrows diversity. Consequently, frontier training has favored reinforcement learning with verifiable external rewards in domains like math and code, alongside human- and environment-grounded feedback for everything else.

noweb.answer: Traditional competitive self-play succeeded in closed-world games like Go because fixed rules provide an exact, incorruptible win-loss signal and a symmetric arena where beating stronger copies guarantees genuine skill improvement. Open-ended language lacks all of these properties. Most LLM tasks are cooperative and asymmetric rather than zero-sum, and they lack an objective, automated verifier for truth, nuance, or helpfulness. When models instead rely on another LLM as a judge or opponent, self-play quickly succumbs to reward hacking, sycophancy, and shared blind spots: policies optimize to exploit the judge's quirks rather than real-world quality, leading to stylistic drift or mode collapse. Moreover, competitive dynamics cannot conjure external factual knowledge from thin air, and human preferences are multi-dimensional and often non-transitive, meaning game-theoretic equilibria do not reliably align with general utility. Consequently, frontier labs have largely favored reinforcement learning against verifiable environments—such as code execution, formal proofs, and math—or curated synthetic data pipelines, where external grounding prevents self-referential drift.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Competitive self-play can generate an endless stream of opponents, but it works best when the environment supplies a reliable measure of progress. In Go, fixed rules determine who wins, and stronger opponents naturally make the game harder. For general language tasks, correctness, usefulness, and factual accuracy often depend on evidence or human judgment outside the interaction. Having two models compete generates more examples, but it doesn’t establish which answers deserve reward.

If a model judges the competition, the players can learn to exploit its blind spots. Models with shared misconceptions can reinforce them, and a rising win rate against other versions of the same model can reflect better tactics in that contest without improving performance on real tasks. Self-play remains useful in domains with reliable checks, such as formal proof or coding against robust tests. For broad LLM training, it can scale the supply of practice, while trustworthy feedback remains the bottleneck.

Competitive self-play works in games because the rules determine who won, and stronger opponents keep the challenge growing. Frontier LLMs face open-ended tasks where winning is often a poor proxy for being right. In a debate, for example, a model can become better at persuading the judge without becoming more factually accurate.

Self-play also generates a curriculum from what the models already know and do. They can discover new strategies, but they can also reinforce shared blind spots or specialize in beating one another. More rounds then produce more interactions without necessarily broadening the skills being learned or supplying missing facts about the world.

Self-play is therefore most useful where success can be checked independently, as with a proof checker. The obstacle to data-free scaling is finding an equally reliable signal across the full range of tasks a general-purpose model must perform.
